claim: After nerve injury, myelin and Remak Schwann cells reprogram to repair cells specialized for regeneration.
source: After nerve injury, myelin and Remak Schwann cells reprogram to repair cells specialized for regeneration.
evidence: This is a well-established finding in the field, supported by citations throughout the manuscript and presented as background knowledge.

claim: Repair cells fail in aging animals, impairing axonal regeneration.
source: Normally providing strong regenerative support, these cells fail in aging animals, and during chronic denervation that results from slow axon growth.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript and citations to previous work.

claim: Repair cells fail during chronic denervation that results from slow axon growth.
source: Normally providing strong regenerative support, these cells fail in aging animals, and during chronic denervation that results from slow axon growth.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in the manuscript and previous literature.

claim: Repair cells express reduced c-Jun protein as regenerative support declines during aging.
source: In mice, we find that repair cells express reduced c-Jun protein as regenerative support provided by these cells declines during aging and chronic denervation.
evidence: This is directly supported by western blot and immunofluorescence data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Repair cells express reduced c-Jun protein as regenerative support declines during chronic denervation.
source: In mice, we find that repair cells express reduced c-Jun protein as regenerative support provided by these cells declines during aging and chronic denervation.
evidence: This is directly supported by western blot and immunofluorescence data presented in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Genetically restoring Schwann cell c-Jun levels restores regeneration to control levels during aging.
source: In both cases, genetically restoring Schwann cell c-Jun levels restores regeneration to control levels.
evidence: This is supported by neuron back-filling experiments and axon counts in c-Jun OE/+ mice shown in Figure 1.

claim: Genetically restoring Schwann cell c-Jun levels restores regeneration to control levels during chronic denervation.
source: In both cases, genetically restoring Schwann cell c-Jun levels restores regeneration to control levels.
evidence: This is supported by neuron back-filling experiments and axon counts in c-Jun OE/+ mice shown in Figure 5.

claim: Shh is implicated in the control of Schwann cell c-Jun levels.
source: We identify potential gene candidates mediating this effect and implicate Shh in the control of Schwann cell c-Jun levels.
evidence: This is supported by experiments with Shh cKO mice and Shh agonists/antagonists shown in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: A common mechanism, reduced c-Jun in Schwann cells, regulates success and failure of nerve repair during both aging and chronic denervation.
source: This establishes that a common mechanism, reduced c-Jun in Schwann cells, regulates success and failure of nerve repair both during aging and chronic denervation.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental data comparing aging and chronic denervation models.

claim: The clinical outcome of nerve injuries remains poor.
source: Yet, paradoxically, the clinical outcome of nerve injuries remains poor, and nerve damage constitutes a significant clinical and economic burden.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to clinical literature.

claim: Treatment of nerve injuries has not advanced significantly for decades.
source: Remarkably, treatment of nerve injuries has not advanced significantly for decades (Furey et al., 2007; Jonsson et al., 2013; reviewed in Fu and Gordon, 1995; Boyd and Gordon, 2003a; Höke, 2006; Allodi et al., 2012; Scheib and Höke, 2013; Doron-Mandel et al., 2015; Jessen and Mirsky, 2016; Fawcett and Verhaagen, 2018; Jessen and Arthur-Farraj, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to review articles and clinical studies.

claim: Increasing age results in a marked decrease in nerve regeneration.
source: One is the age of the animal at the time of injury, increasing age resulting in a marked decrease in regeneration.
evidence: This is supported by citations and experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Chronic denervation causes the nerve distal to injury to gradually lose the capacity to support axon growth.
source: The other is the adverse effect of chronic denervation on the nerve distal to injury, since this tissue gradually loses the capacity to support axon growth as it lies denervated during the often extensive time it takes regenerating axons to reach their targets.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figures 2 and 5, and citations to previous work.

claim: Both aging and chronic denervation involve a common factor, namely a repair Schwann cell failure.
source: These two problems turn out to involve a common factor, namely a repair Schwann cell failure, since both during aging and chronic denervation, the denervated Schwann cells in the distal stump undergo molecular and morphological changes that result in a striking functional deterioration of these important drivers of axonal regeneration (reviewed in Verdú et al., 2000; Sulaiman and Gordon, 2009; Painter, 2017; Jessen and Mirsky, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript and citations to review articles.

claim: c-Jun is upregulated in Schwann cells in injured nerves.
source: That this might be so, is based on our previous finding that c-Jun, which is upregulated in Schwann cells in injured nerves, is a global amplifier of the repair Schwann cell phenotype (Arthur-Farraj et al., 2012; reviewed in Jessen and Mirsky, 2016; Jessen and Mirsky, 2019; Jessen and Arthur-Farraj, 2019)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work and data in the current manuscript.

claim: c-Jun is a global amplifier of the repair Schwann cell phenotype.
source: That this might be so, is based on our previous finding that c-Jun, which is upregulated in Schwann cells in injured nerves, is a global amplifier of the repair Schwann cell phenotype (Arthur-Farraj et al., 2012; reviewed in Jessen and Mirsky, 2016; Jessen and Mirsky, 2019; Jessen and Arthur-Farraj, 2019)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: Enhanced Schwann cell c-Jun promotes regeneration through nerve grafts.
source: and on subsequent findings showing that enhanced Schwann cell c-Jun promotes regeneration, both through nerve grafts and in vitro (Arthur-Farraj et al., 2012; Huang et al., 2015; Huang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Enhanced Schwann cell c-Jun promotes regeneration in vitro.
source: and on subsequent findings showing that enhanced Schwann cell c-Jun promotes regeneration, both through nerve grafts and in vitro (Arthur-Farraj et al., 2012; Huang et al., 2015; Huang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The age-dependent decline in regenerative capacity of human and animal nerves is well established.
source: The age-dependent decline in regenerative capacity of human and animal nerves is well established (Pestronk et al., 1980; Tanaka and deF. Webster, 1991; Tanaka et al., 1992; Graciarena et al., 2014; reviewed in Vaughan, 1992; Verdú et al., 2000; Ruijs et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Age-dependent decline in regeneration is associated with a reduced initial inflammatory response followed by enhanced chronic inflammation.
source: This is associated with a reduced initial inflammatory response followed by enhanced chronic inflammation (Scheib and Höke, 2016; Büttner et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Diminished regeneration during aging is not caused by age-dependent changes in neurons.
source: Interestingly, diminished regeneration is not caused by age-dependent changes in neurons.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Aging results in subdued activation of the repair Schwann cell phenotype after injury, including reduced c-Jun expression, resulting in regeneration failure.
source: Rather, aging results in subdued activation of the repair Schwann cell phenotype after injury, including reduced c-Jun expression, resulting in regeneration failure (Painter et al., 2014; reviewed in Painter, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work and data in the current manuscript.

claim: Chronic denervation results in reduced expression of repair-associated genes including Gdnf, Bdnf, Ntf3, and Ngfr.
source: This is an important issue in human nerve regeneration (Ruijs et al., 2005) and has been studied in some detail in rats, revealing that chronic denervation results in reduced expression of repair-associated genes including Gdnf, Bdnf, Ntf3, and Ngfr, accompanied by a dramatic reduction in the ability of denervated distal stumps to support regeneration even of freshly transected axons (Fu and Gordon, 1995; You et al., 1997; Sulaiman and Gordon, 2000; Höke et al., 2002; Michalski et al., 2008; Eggers et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies in rats and data in the current manuscript.

claim: Chronic denervation results in a dramatic reduction in the ability of denervated distal stumps to support regeneration even of freshly transected axons.
source: This is an important issue in human nerve regeneration (Ruijs et al., 2005) and has been studied in some detail in rats, revealing that chronic denervation results in reduced expression of repair-associated genes including Gdnf, Bdnf, Ntf3, and Ngfr, accompanied by a dramatic reduction in the ability of denervated distal stumps to support regeneration even of freshly transected axons (Fu and Gordon, 1995; You et al., 1997; Sulaiman and Gordon, 2000; Höke et al., 2002; Michalski et al., 2008; Eggers et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies and data in Figure 2.

claim: There is direct evidence for a comparable deterioration of repair cells and repair capacity during chronic denervation of human nerves.
source: There is direct evidence for a comparable deterioration of repair cells and repair capacity during chronic denervation of human nerves (Wilcox et al., 2020; reviewed in Ruijs et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on human nerves.

claim: Chronic denervation results in reduced repair cell numbers and shortening of repair cells.
source: Chronic denervation also results in reduced repair cell numbers and shortening of repair cells (Benito et al., 2017; Gomez-Sanchez et al., 2017; reviewed in Jessen and Mirsky, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work and data in Figure 6.

claim: The repair phenotype is not stable but fades with time after injury.
source: Thus, the repair phenotype is not stable but fades with time after injury, thereby contributing to the poor outcome after nerve damage in humans.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data on chronic denervation presented in the manuscript.

claim: Schwann cell reprograming after nerve injury involves upregulation of trophic factors and cytokines.
source: Schwann cell reprograming after nerve injury involves upregulation of trophic factors and cytokines, activation of EMT genes, and myelin autophagy for myelin clearance and downregulation of myelin genes (Brushart et al., 2013; Arthur-Farraj et al., 2017; Clements et al., 2017; reviewed in Gröthe et al., 2006; Chen et al., 2007; Gambarotta et al., 2013; Glenn and Talbot, 2013; Jessen and Mirsky, 2016; Boerboom et al., 2017; Jessen and Arthur-Farraj, 2019; Nocera and Jacob, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Schwann cell reprograming after nerve injury involves activation of EMT genes.
source: Schwann cell reprograming after nerve injury involves upregulation of trophic factors and cytokines, activation of EMT genes, and myelin autophagy for myelin clearance and downregulation of myelin genes (Brushart et al., 2013; Arthur-Farraj et al., 2017; Clements et al., 2017; reviewed in Gröthe et al., 2006; Chen et al., 2007; Gambarotta et al., 2013; Glenn and Talbot, 2013; Jessen and Mirsky, 2016; Boerboom et al., 2017; Jessen and Arthur-Farraj, 2019; Nocera and Jacob, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Schwann cell reprograming after nerve injury involves myelin autophagy for myelin clearance.
source: Schwann cell reprograming after nerve injury involves upregulation of trophic factors and cytokines, activation of EMT genes, and myelin autophagy for myelin clearance and downregulation of myelin genes (Brushart et al., 2013; Arthur-Farraj et al., 2017; Clements et al., 2017; reviewed in Gröthe et al., 2006; Chen et al., 2007; Gambarotta et al., 2013; Glenn and Talbot, 2013; Jessen and Mirsky, 2016; Boerboom et al., 2017; Jessen and Arthur-Farraj, 2019; Nocera and Jacob, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Schwann cell reprograming after nerve injury involves downregulation of myelin genes.
source: Schwann cell reprograming after nerve injury involves upregulation of trophic factors and cytokines, activation of EMT genes, and myelin autophagy for myelin clearance and downregulation of myelin genes (Brushart et al., 2013; Arthur-Farraj et al., 2017; Clements et al., 2017; reviewed in Gröthe et al., 2006; Chen et al., 2007; Gambarotta et al., 2013; Glenn and Talbot, 2013; Jessen and Mirsky, 2016; Boerboom et al., 2017; Jessen and Arthur-Farraj, 2019; Nocera and Jacob, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Myelin and Remak Schwann cells increase in length by two-to-three fold as they convert to repair cells.
source: Myelin and Remak Schwann cells also increase in length by two-to-three fold and often branch as they convert to repair cells and form regeneration tracks, Bungner bands, that guide regenerating axons (Gomez-Sanchez et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Repair cells form regeneration tracks, Bungner bands, that guide regenerating axons.
source: Myelin and Remak Schwann cells also increase in length by two-to-three fold and often branch as they convert to repair cells and form regeneration tracks, Bungner bands, that guide regenerating axons (Gomez-Sanchez et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work and is established knowledge.

claim: The molecular signals involved in the decline of repair-supportive features during aging and chronic denervation have not been known.
source: The molecular signals involved in the decline of these repair-supportive features during aging and chronic denervation have not been known.
evidence: This statement sets up the rationale for the current study.

claim: c-Jun regulates the reprograming of myelin and Remak cells to repair cells by accelerating the extinction of myelin genes.
source: The transcription factor c-Jun regulates the reprograming of myelin and Remak cells to repair cells by accelerating the extinction of myelin genes, promoting myelin breakdown, and by amplifying the upregulation of a broad spectrum of repair-supportive features, including the expression of trophic factors.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: c-Jun promotes myelin breakdown.
source: The transcription factor c-Jun regulates the reprograming of myelin and Remak cells to repair cells by accelerating the extinction of myelin genes, promoting myelin breakdown, and by amplifying the upregulation of a broad spectrum of repair-supportive features, including the expression of trophic factors.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: c-Jun amplifies the upregulation of a broad spectrum of repair-supportive features, including the expression of trophic factors.
source: The transcription factor c-Jun regulates the reprograming of myelin and Remak cells to repair cells by accelerating the extinction of myelin genes, promoting myelin breakdown, and by amplifying the upregulation of a broad spectrum of repair-supportive features, including the expression of trophic factors.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: Genetic removal of c-Jun from Schwann cells results in functionally impaired repair cells and regeneration failure.
source: Accordingly, genetic removal of c-Jun from Schwann cells results in functionally impaired repair cells and regeneration failure (Arthur-Farraj et al., 2012; Fontana et al., 2012; reviewed in Jessen and Arthur-Farraj, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Four days after transection, c-Jun protein levels in the distal nerve stump in aged mice (8–10 months) were ~50% lower than in young (6–8 weeks) mice.
source: Four days after transection, c-Jun protein levels in the distal nerve stump in aged mice (8–10 months) were found to be ~50% lower than in young (6–8 weeks) mice.
evidence: This is directly supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: In c-Jun OE/+ mice, the age-dependent decline in c-Jun protein levels after sciatic nerve cut was prevented.
source: We found that in c-Jun OE/+ mice, the age-dependent decline in c-Jun protein levels after sciatic nerve cut was prevented, and that c-Jun levels in the distal stump of young WT and aging c-Jun OE/+ mice were similar by western blots 4 days after cut (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is directly supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: c-Jun levels in the distal stump of young WT and aging c-Jun OE/+ mice were similar by western blots 4 days after cut.
source: We found that in c-Jun OE/+ mice, the age-dependent decline in c-Jun protein levels after sciatic nerve cut was prevented, and that c-Jun levels in the distal stump of young WT and aging c-Jun OE/+ mice were similar by western blots 4 days after cut (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is directly supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: There was a significant elevation of c-Jun mRNA in cut c-Jun OE/+ nerves.
source: At the mRNA level, a non-significant trend towards lower c-Jun expression was seen in 3-day cut nerves of aged WT nerves, while there was a significant elevation of c-Jun mRNA in cut c-Jun OE/+ nerves as expected (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is directly supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: In WT mice, older nerves contained fewer c-Jun-positive Schwann cell nuclei and the labeling of the c-Jun-positive nuclei was weaker, compared to young nerves.
source: In WT mice, older nerves contained fewer c-Jun-positive Schwann cell nuclei and the labeling of the c-Jun-positive nuclei was weaker, compared to young nerves.
evidence: This is directly supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: In aged c-Jun OE/+ nerves nuclear c-Jun was restored to levels similar to those in young WT nerves.
source: In aged c-Jun OE/+ nerves nuclear c-Jun was restored to levels similar to those in young WT nerves.
evidence: This is directly supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The number of neurons regenerating through the distal stump of aged WT mice was reduced by about 50% compared to young mice.
source: The number of neurons regenerating through the distal stump of aged WT mice was reduced by about 50% compared to young mice.
evidence: This is directly supported by neuron back-filling data shown in Figure 1D and E.

claim: In aged c-Jun OE/+ mice, regeneration of DRG and motor neurons was restored to levels similar to those in young WT nerves.
source: In aged c-Jun OE/+ mice on the other hand, regeneration of DRG and motor neurons was restored to levels similar to those in young WT nerves.
evidence: This is directly supported by neuron back-filling data shown in Figure 1D and E.

claim: The number of CGRP+ fibers were reduced in aged WT nerves compared to young ones, but increased in the aged c-Jun OE/+ nerves.
source: In confirmation, counts of CGRP+ fibers in the sciatic nerve were performed 3 days after nerve crush, 3 mm from the injury site (Figure 1F). The number of fibers were reduced in aged WT nerves compared to young ones, but increased in the aged c-Jun OE/+ nerves.
evidence: This is directly supported by axon count data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Restoration of c-Jun elevation selectively in Schwann cells to that seen in young animals is sufficient to restore nerve regeneration to youthful levels.
source: Importantly, restoration of c-Jun elevation selectively in Schwann cells to that seen in young animals is sufficient to restore nerve regeneration to youthful levels.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Figure 1.

claim: mRNA levels for genes associated with denervated Schwann cells (S100b, Ngfr, Gdnf, and sonic hedgehog (Shh)) declined substantially between 1 and 10 weeks of denervation.
source: mRNA levels for genes associated with denervated Schwann cells (S100b, Ngfr, Gdnf, and sonic hedgehog (Shh)) declined substantially between 1 and 10 weeks of denervation (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is directly supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Western blots of p75NTR (Ngfr) in the distal stump showed a rise to a maximum 1 week after injury and a decline thereafter to <50% of peak levels at 10 weeks.
source: Western blots of p75NTR (Ngfr) in the distal stump showed a rise to a maximum 1 week after injury and a decline thereafter to <50% of peak levels at 10 weeks (Figure 2B) in line with that seen in rat (You et al., 1997).
evidence: This is directly supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2B and is consistent with previous work in rats.

claim: Only about half as many spinal cord motor neurons projected into the 10-week denervated stumps compared to the acutely transected stumps.
source: Only about half as many spinal cord motor neurons projected into the 10-week denervated stumps compared to the acutely transected stumps (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is directly supported by neuron back-filling data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Ten-week denervated stumps contained many fewer regenerating neurofilament labeled axons than nerve stumps sutured immediately after transection.
source: Failure of regeneration through 10-week denervated stumps was confirmed by immunohistochemistry and counting of neurofilament-positive axons in similar experiments. Ten-week denervated stumps contained many fewer regenerating neurofilament labeled axons than nerve stumps sutured immediately after transection (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is directly supported by axon count data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The capacity of the distal stump to support regeneration declines between 1 and 10 weeks of denervation.
source: This shows that the capacity of the distal stump to support regeneration declines between 1 and 10 weeks of denervation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the neuron back-filling data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: c-Jun protein levels in distal stumps showed strong elevation 3 days and 1 week after sciatic nerve cut followed by a decline to ~40% of 1 week levels at 10 weeks.
source: Measuring c-Jun protein levels in distal stumps showed strong elevation 3 days and 1 week after sciatic nerve cut followed by a decline to ~40% of 1 week levels at 10 weeks (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is directly supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The c-Jun shown in western blots represented c-Jun in Schwann cells.
source: We verified that the c-Jun shown in these western blots represented c-Jun in Schwann cells, using mice with conditional c-Jun inactivation selectively in Schwann cells (Arthur-Farraj et al., 2012; Figure 3B).
evidence: This is directly supported by western blot data from c-Jun cKO mice shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Ten-week denervated stumps showed many more c-Jun negative, Sox10-positive nuclei, and the c-Jun labeling, where present, was also weaker.
source: Further, 1- and 10-week denervated stumps were compared using double immunofluorescent labeling with c-Jun antibodies and Sox10 antibodies to selectively identify Schwann cell nuclei. Ten-week denervated stumps showed many more c-Jun negative, Sox10-positive nuclei, and the c-Jun labeling, where present, was also weaker (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is directly supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The decline in c-Jun and p75NTR expression after long-term denervation in vivo was mimicked in purified Schwann cells in vitro.
source: The decline in c-Jun and p75NTR expression after long-term denervation in vivo was mimicked in purified Schwann cells in vitro.
evidence: This is directly supported by western blot and immunofluorescence data from cultured Schwann cells shown in Figure 3D-F.

claim: Cells that had been maintained ~6 weeks in vitro (nine passages), contained less c-Jun and p75NTR protein compared to cells maintained ~10 days in vitro (two passages).
source: By western blots, cells that had been maintained ~6 weeks in vitro (nine passages), contained less c-Jun and p75NTR protein compared to cells maintained ~10 days in vitro (two passages) (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is directly supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The levels of c-Jun mRNA declined in long-term Schwann cell cultures.
source: The levels of c-Jun mRNA also declined in long-term cultures (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is directly supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The decline in c-Jun and p75NTR during chronic denervation is not driven by endoneurial signals.
source: These in vitro experiments suggest that the decline in c-Jun and p75NTR during chronic denervation is not driven by endoneurial signals.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the in vitro data showing similar decline in isolated Schwann cells.

claim: One- and 3-week denervated distal stumps of c-Jun OE/+ and WT mice contained similar c-Jun protein levels.
source: One- and 3-week denervated distal stumps of c-Jun OE/+ and WT mice contained similar c-Jun protein levels.
evidence: This is directly supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: At 10 weeks, when c-Jun had declined in WT mice, c-Jun was maintained in c-Jun OE/+ mice at levels similar to those at 1 week.
source: However, at 10 weeks, when c-Jun had declined in WT mice, c-Jun was maintained in c-Jun OE/+ mice at levels similar to those at 1 week (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is directly supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: At 1 week, the c-Jun labeling of Sox10-positive nuclei in WT and c-Jun OE/+ mice was comparable, but reduced at 10 weeks in WT nerves only.
source: This showed similar c-Jun nuclear labeling in 1-week denervated stumps of WT and c-Jun OE/+ mice, while at 10 weeks, WT nerves showed a reduced number of c-Jun-positive nuclei and decreased labeling intensity. This decrease was prevented in c-Jun OE/+ nerves.
evidence: This is directly supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: In 1- to 3-week cut nerves, the maximum capacity of Schwann cells to express c-Jun protein is already reached in the WT, both genotypes showing a similar 80–100 fold elevation after injury.
source: These experiments indicate that in 1- to 3-week cut nerves, the maximum capacity of Schwann cells to express c-Jun protein is already reached in the WT, both genotypes showing a similar 80–100 fold elevation after injury.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the western blot data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: During chronic denervation, high c-Jun expression levels fall substantially in WT nerves, but not in c-Jun OE/+ nerves.
source: During chronic denervation, these high expression levels fall substantially in WT nerves, but not in c-Jun OE/+ nerves.
evidence: This is directly supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: In WT mice, the number of DRG neurons projecting through 10-week cut nerves was only about half that projecting through acutely cut nerves.
source: In WT mice, the number of DRG neurons projecting through 10-week cut nerves was only about half that projecting through acutely cut nerves.
evidence: This is directly supported by neuron back-filling data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: In 10-week cut c-Jun OE/+ nerves, the drop in regenerating DRG neurons was not seen.
source: In 10-week cut c-Jun OE/+ nerves, however, this drop was not seen (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is directly supported by neuron back-filling data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Both DRG and motor neurons regenerated as well through 10-week denervated c-Jun OE/+ nerves as they did through acutely cut WT nerves.
source: Thus, both DRG and motor neurons regenerated as well through 10-week denervated c-Jun OE/+ nerves as they did through acutely cut WT nerves, suggesting that c-Jun OE/+ Schwann cells maintain their capacity to support regenerating neurons despite chronic denervation.
evidence: This is directly supported by neuron back-filling data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: c-Jun OE/+ Schwann cells maintain their capacity to support regenerating neurons despite chronic denervation.
source: Thus, both DRG and motor neurons regenerated as well through 10-week denervated c-Jun OE/+ nerves as they did through acutely cut WT nerves, suggesting that c-Jun OE/+ Schwann cells maintain their capacity to support regenerating neurons despite chronic denervation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the neuron back-filling data.

claim: Nearly three times more neurofilament+ fibers were found in 10-week denervated c-Jun OE/+ nerves compared to 10-week denervated WT nerves.
source: In confirmation, regeneration into 10-week denervated distal stumps of the tibial nerve was examined with neurofilament staining, 1 week after the stumps were sutured to freshly cut peroneal nerves. Nearly three times more fibers were found in 10-week denervated c-Jun OE/+ nerves compared to 10-week denervated WT nerves (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is directly supported by axon count data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The number of back-filled DRG and motor neurons in c-Jun OE/+ mice was similar to that in WT animals when tracer was applied immediately after transection.
source: First, peroneal nerves in WT and c-Jun OE/+ mice were transected followed by immediate application of tracer to the injured proximal stump. The number of back-filled DRG and motor neurons in c-Jun OE/+ mice was similar to that in WT animals (Figure 5D,E).
evidence: This is directly supported by neuron back-filling data shown in Figure 5D and E.

claim: The regeneration support provided by WT and c-Jun OE/+ nerves was similar early after injury.
source: In line with this, the regeneration support provided by WT and c-Jun OE/+ nerves was similar early after injury.
evidence: This is supported by neuron back-filling data shown in Figure 5F and G.

claim: No significant difference was seen between WT and c-Jun OE/+ mice in the numbers of DRG or motor neurons that regenerated through acutely transected distal stumps (immediate repair) when the tracer was applied 2 weeks after transection/repair.
source: Thus, in back-filling experiments no significant difference was seen between WT and c-Jun OE/+ mice in the numbers of DRG or motor neurons that regenerated through acutely transected distal stumps (immediate repair) when the tracer was applied 2 weeks after transection/repair (Figure 5F and not shown).
evidence: This is directly supported by neuron back-filling data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Comparable numbers of back-filled motor neurons were obtained in WT and c-Jun OE/+ mice when back-filling was used to quantify regeneration 5 days after sciatic nerve crush.
source: Similarly, comparable numbers of back-filled motor neurons were obtained in WT and c-Jun OE/+ mice when back-filling was used to quantify regeneration 5 days after sciatic nerve crush (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is directly supported by neuron back-filling data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Under the conditions prevailing in the distal stump of cut nerves, Schwann cells are unable to maintain high c-Jun levels in the long term.
source: Together, these experiments indicate that under the conditions prevailing in the distal stump of cut nerves, Schwann cells are unable to maintain high c-Jun levels in the long term.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on chronic denervation.

claim: The gradual reduction in c-Jun leads to deterioration of repair cell function, causing regeneration failure.
source: The resulting gradual reduction in c-Jun leads to deterioration of repair cell function, causing regeneration failure, a failure that can be corrected by restoring c-Jun levels.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing restoration of regeneration in c-Jun OE/+ mice.

claim: Regeneration failure caused by chronic denervation can be corrected by restoring c-Jun levels.
source: The resulting gradual reduction in c-Jun leads to deterioration of repair cell function, causing regeneration failure, a failure that can be corrected by restoring c-Jun levels.
evidence: This is directly supported by the regeneration data in c-Jun OE/+ mice shown in Figure 5.

claim: Schwann cell and macrophage numbers and density were similar irrespective of genotype or age in experiments comparing young and aging animals.
source: Schwann cell and macrophage numbers and density were similar irrespective of genotype or age (Figure 6A–C).
evidence: This is directly supported by electron microscopy cell count data shown in Figure 6A-C.

claim: There was some decrease in fibroblast density in aged mice, but density and numbers were similar irrespective of genotype.
source: There was some decrease in fibroblast density in aged mice, but density and numbers were similar irrespective of genotype (Figure 6D,E).
evidence: This is directly supported by electron microscopy cell count data shown in Figure 6D and E.

claim: In aged mice, transverse profiles of the tibial nerve were larger mainly because of increased endoneurial connective tissue, but no difference was seen between the genotypes.
source: In aged mice, transverse profiles of the tibial nerve were larger mainly because of increased endoneurial connective tissue, but no difference was seen between the genotypes (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is directly supported by nerve area measurements shown in Figure 6F.

claim: There were ~250 Schwann cell nuclei in 2-week stumps, representing a ~2.5-fold increase from uninjured nerves.
source: There were ~250 Schwann cell nuclei in 2-week stumps, representing a ~2.5-fold increase from uninjured nerves (Fazal et al., 2017; Figure 6G).
evidence: This is directly supported by electron microscopy cell count data shown in Figure 6G and a citation to previous work.

claim: In the WT, Schwann cell numbers declined by ~30% during chronic denervation.
source: In the WT, Schwann cell numbers declined by ~30% during chronic denervation.
evidence: This is directly supported by electron microscopy cell count data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: The drop in Schwann cell numbers during chronic denervation was prevented in c-Jun OE/+ nerves.
source: This drop was prevented in c-Jun OE/+ nerves (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is directly supported by electron microscopy cell count data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: The density of macrophages was similar irrespective of genotype or length of denervation.
source: The density of macrophages was similar irrespective of genotype or length of denervation (Figure 6H), with numbers declining, irrespective of genotype, during chronic denervation (Figure 6I).
evidence: This is directly supported by electron microscopy cell count data shown in Figure 6H and I.

claim: Macrophage numbers declined, irrespective of genotype, during chronic denervation.
source: The density of macrophages was similar irrespective of genotype or length of denervation (Figure 6H), with numbers declining, irrespective of genotype, during chronic denervation (Figure 6I).
evidence: This is directly supported by electron microscopy cell count data shown in Figure 6I.

claim: Two weeks after injury, fibroblast density in WT and c-Jun OE/+ mice was similar.
source: Two weeks after injury, fibroblast density in WT and c-Jun OE/+ mice was similar.
evidence: This is directly supported by electron microscopy cell count data shown in Figure 6J.

claim: Fibroblast density was elevated in 10-week stumps of WT, but not c-Jun OE/+, mice.
source: Fibroblast density was elevated in 10-week stumps of WT, but not c-Jun OE/+, mice (Figure 6J).
evidence: This is directly supported by electron microscopy cell count data shown in Figure 6J.

claim: Fibroblast numbers remained unchanged between genotypes following denervation.
source: Fibroblast numbers remained unchanged between genotypes following denervation (Figure 6K).
evidence: This is directly supported by electron microscopy cell count data shown in Figure 6K.

claim: Chronically denervated stumps of both genotypes had reduced nerve area, although this difference was less evident in c-Jun OE/+ nerves.
source: Chronically denervated stumps of both genotypes had reduced nerve area, although this difference was less evident in c-Jun OE/+ nerves (Figure 6L).
evidence: This is directly supported by nerve area measurements shown in Figure 6L.

claim: Altered cell numbers are not a significant reason for improved regeneration in aged c-Jun OE/+ nerves.
source: These counts indicate that altered cell numbers are not a significant reason for improved regeneration in aged c-Jun OE/+ nerves.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the cell count data in Figure 6.

claim: In chronically denervated nerves, the normal loss of Schwann cells in WT nerves is prevented in c-Jun OE/+ nerves.
source: In chronically denervated nerves, the normal loss of Schwann cells in WT nerves is prevented in c-Jun OE/+ nerves.
evidence: This is directly supported by cell count data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Even in 10-week WT stumps, Schwann cell numbers remain well above those in uninjured nerves.
source: Even in 10-week WT stumps, however, cell numbers remain well above those in uninjured nerves (see Discussion).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cell count data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Shh is not expressed in developing Schwann cells or in intact nerves, but strongly upregulated in repair Schwann cells after injury.
source: Seeking mechanisms that promote c-Jun expression in denervated Schwann cells, we considered signaling by Shh, a gene that is not expressed in developing Schwann cells or in intact nerves, but strongly upregulated in repair Schwann cells after injury (Lu et al., 2000; Zhou et al., 2000; Arthur-Farraj et al., 2012; Hsin-Pin et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In Shh cKO mice, c-Jun protein and phosphorylated c-Jun were decreased in the distal stump of 7-day transected sciatic nerve.
source: We found that in the mutants, c-Jun protein and phosphorylated c-Jun were decreased in the distal stump of 7-day transected sciatic nerve (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: This is directly supported by western blot data shown in Figure 7A and B.

claim: Levels of p75NTR protein were reduced 7 days after injury in Shh cKO mutants.
source: Levels of p75NTR protein, which is positively regulated by c-Jun in Schwann cells (Arthur-Farraj et al., 2012), were also reduced 7 days after injury in the mutants (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is directly supported by western blot data shown in Figure 7C and a citation to previous work.

claim: Two Shh signaling agonists, SAG and purmorphamine, upregulated c-Jun protein in purified Schwann cell cultures.
source: Substantiating these observations, two Shh signaling agonists, SAG and purmorphamine, upregulated c-Jun protein in purified Schwann cell cultures (Figure 7D,E).
evidence: This is directly supported by western blot data shown in Figure 7D and E.

claim: SAG promoted the elongated bi- or tri-polar shape in vitro that reflects the elongation and branching of repair cells in vivo.
source: Further, SAG promoted another effect of c-Jun, that of enhancing the elongated bi- or tri-polar shape in vitro that reflects the elongation and branching of repair cells in vivo (Arthur-Farraj et al., 2012; Gomez-Sanchez et al., 2017; Figure 8C).
evidence: This is directly supported by morphological analysis shown in Figure 8C and citations to previous work.

claim: Cyclopamine alone downregulated c-Jun protein and sharply suppressed c-Jun phosphorylation in cultured Schwann cells.
source: In support of such an autocrine hedgehog signaling loop, cyclopamine alone, which blocks cellular responses to Shh, downregulated c-Jun protein and sharply suppressed c-Jun phosphorylation in cultured Schwann cells (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is directly supported by western blot data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Shh promotes Schwann cell c-Jun expression in vitro and in vivo.
source: Together these observations show that Shh promotes Schwann cell c-Jun expression in vitro and in vivo, and support the idea that injury triggers an autocrine Shh signaling loop to elevate c-Jun in repair cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: Injury triggers an autocrine Shh signaling loop to elevate c-Jun in repair cells.
source: Together these observations show that Shh promotes Schwann cell c-Jun expression in vitro and in vivo, and support the idea that injury triggers an autocrine Shh signaling loop to elevate c-Jun in repair cells.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing effects of Shh agonists and antagonists.

claim: In uninjured WT nerves, 1477 genes were differentially expressed between young and aged mice.
source: In uninjured WT nerves, out of 15,995 genes present, 1477 genes were differentially expressed between young and aged mice. Of these, 1154 were upregulated and 323 downregulated in aging mice compared to young ones (FC >2; and FDR 0.05) (Supplementary file 1 A; Supplementary file 2 A).
evidence: This is directly supported by RNA sequencing data analysis.

claim: 138 of the 173 c-Jun-regulated injury genes were present in the aging data set.
source: We tested whether the 173 genes we previously identified as c-Jun-regulated injury genes (Arthur-Farraj et al., 2012) were implicated in these age-dependent differences. In the present data set, 138 of the 173 genes were present (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is directly supported by RNA sequencing data analysis and a citation to previous work.

claim: The 138 c-Jun-regulated genes showed a strong enrichment among the 1477 genes differentially expressed between young and aging mice.
source: They showed a strong enrichment among the 1477 genes differentially expressed between young and aging mice (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is directly supported by over-representation analysis shown in Figure 9A.

claim: In 3-day cut WT nerves, 398 genes were differentially expressed between young and aging mice.
source: In 3-day cut WT nerves, of 17,334 genes present, 398 genes were differentially expressed between young and aging mice. Of these, 268 were upregulated and 130 downregulated in aging nerves (Supplementary file 1 B; Supplementary file 2 B).
evidence: This is directly supported by RNA sequencing data analysis.

claim: Trophic factors such as GDNF, BDNF, NGF, erythropoietin, and FGF were not among the differentially expressed genes between young and aged 3-day cut nerves.
source: In agreement with Painter et al., 2014, trophic factors such as GDNF, BDNF, NGF, erythropoietin, and FGF were not among the differentially expressed genes.
evidence: This is directly supported by RNA sequencing data analysis and a citation to previous work.

claim: Expression of trophic factors often implicated in regeneration may not explain different regeneration between young and aged mice.
source: This suggests that expression of trophic factors often implicated in regeneration may not explain different regeneration between young and aged mice.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the RNA sequencing data.

claim: The 138 c-Jun-regulated injury genes were highly enriched among the age-regulated genes in 3-day cut nerves.
source: The 138 c-Jun-regulated injury genes (Supplementary file 3; Arthur-Farraj et al., 2012) were highly enriched among the age-regulated genes (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is directly supported by over-representation analysis shown in Figure 9A.

claim: 822 genes showed significant difference in the injury response when young and aging WT mice were compared.
source: Examining the injury response (3-day cut vs uninjured nerve), 822 genes showed significant difference when young and aging WT mice were compared (Supplementary file 1 C; Supplementary file 2 C).
evidence: This is directly supported by RNA sequencing data analysis.

claim: The 138 c-Jun-regulated injury genes were strongly enriched among the 822 genes showing differential injury response between young and aged mice.
source: The 138 c-Jun-regulated injury genes were strongly enriched among these 822 genes (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is directly supported by over-representation analysis shown in Figure 9A.

claim: The c-Jun-regulated repair program is disproportionately vulnerable during the aging process.
source: These correlations between enrichment of c-Jun-regulated genes and Schwann cell age suggest that the c-Jun-regulated repair program is disproportionately vulnerable during the aging process.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the enrichment analysis of c-Jun genes in aging.

claim: In aged uninjured WT nerves, downregulated genes were largely involved in lipid metabolism, as well as myelination.
source: Gene ontology (GO) analysis showed that in aged uninjured WT nerves, downregulated genes were largely involved in lipid metabolism, as well as myelination, while genes involved in the immune system were prominent among those upregulated (Figure 9B,C; reviewed in Melcangi et al., 1998; Melcangi et al., 2000; Büttner et al., 2018).
evidence: This is directly supported by GO analysis shown in Figure 9B and citations to previous work.

claim: In aged uninjured WT nerves, genes involved in the immune system were prominent among those upregulated.
source: Gene ontology (GO) analysis showed that in aged uninjured WT nerves, downregulated genes were largely involved in lipid metabolism, as well as myelination, while genes involved in the immune system were prominent among those upregulated (Figure 9B,C; reviewed in Melcangi et al., 1998; Melcangi et al., 2000; Büttner et al., 2018).
evidence: This is directly supported by GO analysis shown in Figure 9C and citations to previous work.

claim: In aged WT nerves, the injury response showed reduced activation of immune genes.
source: Similar analysis of the injury response (3-day cut vs uninjured) showed reduced activation of immune genes in aged WT nerves (Scheib and Höke, 2016; Büttner et al., 2018).
evidence: This is directly supported by GO analysis shown in Figure 9D and citations to previous work.

claim: In aged nerves, MAPK pathways were suppressed while lipid metabolism and Schwann cell differentiation genes were enhanced.
source: In aged nerves, MAPK pathways were also suppressed while lipid metabolism and Schwann cell differentiation genes were enhanced (Figure 9D,E).
evidence: This is directly supported by GO analysis shown in Figure 9D and E.

claim: Aged WT nerves show suppressed Schwann cell reprogramming and repair cell activation.
source: Together this indicates suppressed Schwann cell reprogramming and repair cell activation in nerves of older WT mice.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the GO analysis data.

claim: Pathways associated with protein processing and maturation were upregulated in aged c-Jun OE/+ nerves compared with aged WT nerves.
source: Testing the effects of enhanced c-Jun expression on the aged injury response, we found that pathways associated with protein processing and maturation were upregulated in aged c-Jun OE/+ nerves compared with aged WT nerves (Figure 9F).
evidence: This is directly supported by GO analysis shown in Figure 9F.

claim: 303 genes show significant injury response in young WT mice but not in aging WT mice, but are again significantly regulated by restoring c-Jun to youthful levels in aging c-Jun OE/+ mice.
source: Of particular interest are the 303 genes that show significant injury response in young WT mice but not in aging WT mice, but are again significantly regulated by restoring c-Jun to youthful levels in aging c-Jun OE/+ mice (Supplementary file 2 D).
evidence: This is directly supported by RNA sequencing data analysis shown in Figure 9G.

claim: In 3-day cut aged WT nerves, 16 c-Jun-regulated genes were differentially expressed compared to 3-day cut young WT nerves.
source: In 3-day cut aged WT nerves, where regeneration fails, 16 c-Jun-regulated genes were differentially expressed compared to 3-day cut young WT nerves.
evidence: This is directly supported by RNA sequencing data analysis.

claim: Four c-Jun-regulated genes (Aqp5, Gpr37L1, Igfbp2, and Olig1) were restored in aged c-Jun OE/+ nerves, where regeneration is restored.
source: Four of these, Aqp5, Gpr37L1, Igfbp2, and Olig1, were restored in aged c-Jun OE/+ nerves, where regeneration is restored (Figure 9H).
evidence: This is directly supported by RNA sequencing data analysis shown in Figure 9H.

claim: In aging mice, both regeneration failure and the expression defect of Aqp5, Gpr37L1, Igfbp2, and Olig1 was restored to levels in young mice, by elevating c-Jun levels.
source: Thus, in aging mice, both regeneration failure and the expression defect of these four genes was restored to levels in young mice, by elevating c-Jun levels.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the RNA sequencing and regeneration data.

claim: Expression of 1581 genes changed significantly during chronic denervation.
source: Gene expression was examined in uninjured nerves and in 1 and 10-week cut sciatic nerves of WT and c-Jun OE/+ mice (Figure 10—figure supplement 1A). Expression of 1581 genes changed significantly during chronic denervation (Supplementary file 4; Supplementary file 2 E).
evidence: This is directly supported by RNA sequencing data analysis.

claim: In 10-week cut nerves, 601 genes were downregulated, including genes associated with repair cells such as Gdnf, Shh, and Ngfr, while 980 genes were upregulated.
source: In 10-week cut nerves, 601 of these genes were downregulated, including genes associated with repair cells such as Gdnf, Shh, and Ngfr, while 980 genes were upregulated.
evidence: This is directly supported by RNA sequencing data analysis.

claim: The 138 c-Jun-regulated genes showed a highly significant 5.8-fold enrichment among the 1581 genes regulated during chronic denervation.
source: The 138 c-Jun-regulated genes showed a highly significant 5.8-fold enrichment (p=2.2×10−16) among the 1581 genes regulated during chronic denervation.
evidence: This is directly supported by enrichment analysis of RNA sequencing data.

claim: The major genes downregulated during chronic denervation in WT nerves involved the cell cycle, DNA replication, and repair.
source: GO analysis showed that the major genes downregulated during chronic denervation in WT nerves involved the cell cycle, DNA replication, and repair.
evidence: This is directly supported by GO analysis shown in Figure 10A.

claim: Glial cell differentiation genes and MAPK pathways were suppressed during chronic denervation.
source: Glial cell differentiation genes and MAPK pathways, potential activators of c-Jun, were also suppressed (Figure 10A).
evidence: This is directly supported by GO analysis shown in Figure 10A.

claim: Chronic denervation involved a prominent upregulation of neuro-glia signaling genes (chiefly related to GABA and adrenergic signaling), but also regulators of differentiation, Notch and cAMP signaling.
source: Chronic denervation involved a prominent upregulation of neuro-glia signaling genes (chiefly related to GABA and adrenergic signaling), but also regulators of differentiation, Notch and cAMP signaling (Figure 10B).
evidence: This is directly supported by GO analysis shown in Figure 10B.

claim: In chronically denervated c-Jun OE/+ mice, there was strong upregulation of pathways involved in PNS and Schwann cell development and differentiation.
source: To test the effects of maintaining c-Jun protein levels during the 10-week chronic denervation, we identified genes differentially expressed between 10-week cut WT and c-Jun OE/+ nerves (Figure 10C). This showed strong upregulation, in c-Jun OE/+ mice, of pathways involved in PNS and Schwann cell development and differentiation.
evidence: This is directly supported by GO analysis shown in Figure 10C.

claim: 227 genes showed an injury response in WT 1-week nerves and in c-Jun OE/+ 10-week nerves, both of which show fast regeneration, but no injury response in WT 10-week nerves, where regeneration is slow.
source: A point of interest are the 227 genes that showed an injury response in WT 1-week nerves and in c-Jun OE/+ 10-week nerves, both of which show fast regeneration, but no injury response in WT 10-week nerves, where regeneration is slow (Supplementary file 2 F).
evidence: This is directly supported by RNA sequencing data analysis shown in Figure 10D.

claim: Fifty of the 138 c-Jun-regulated genes changed expression during chronic denervation in WT nerves, where regeneration is poor.
source: Fifty of the 138 genes changed expression during chronic denervation in WT nerves, where regeneration is poor.
evidence: This is directly supported by RNA sequencing data analysis.

claim: In chronically denervated c-Jun OE/+ nerves, expression levels of five c-Jun-regulated genes (Cxcl5, Egfl8, Gas213, Megf10, and Pcdh20) were restored, completely or partially.
source: In chronically denervated c-Jun OE/+ nerves, where regeneration is restored, expression levels were restored, completely or partially, in the case of five of these genes, Cxcl5, Egfl8, Gas213, Megf10, and Pcdh20 (Figure 10E).
evidence: This is directly supported by RNA sequencing data analysis shown in Figure 10E.

claim: Reduced expression of c-Jun is an important factor in the repair cell failures seen during aging and chronic denervation.
source: The present results indicate that reduced expression of c-Jun is an important factor in the repair cell failures seen during aging and chronic denervation.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by all the experimental data.

claim: In both aging and chronic denervation, Schwann cells of injured nerves fail to achieve or maintain high c-Jun levels.
source: In both situations, Schwann cells of injured nerves fail to achieve or maintain high c-Jun levels, and in both cases, correction of c-Jun expression restores regeneration deficits.
evidence: This is directly supported by the experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Correction of c-Jun expression restores regeneration deficits in both aging and chronic denervation.
source: In both situations, Schwann cells of injured nerves fail to achieve or maintain high c-Jun levels, and in both cases, correction of c-Jun expression restores regeneration deficits.
evidence: This is directly supported by the experimental data in Figures 1 and 5.

claim: This study provides a common molecular link between two apparently unrelated problems in nerve repair.
source: This highlights the importance of c-Jun in the function of repair Schwann cells, provides a common molecular link between two apparently unrelated problems in nerve repair, and points to manipulation of c-Jun-regulated pathways as a potential route for improving the outcome of nerve injuries.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Manipulation of c-Jun-regulated pathways is a potential route for improving the outcome of nerve injuries.
source: This highlights the importance of c-Jun in the function of repair Schwann cells, provides a common molecular link between two apparently unrelated problems in nerve repair, and points to manipulation of c-Jun-regulated pathways as a potential route for improving the outcome of nerve injuries.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the experimental findings.
